name: ACS780LLRTR-100B-T
title: Linear Hall-effect current sensor with 200 µΩ integrated conductor, 7-pin PSOF
summary: A current sensor IC: the measured current runs through a 200 µΩ copper path inside the package, and a Hall circuit next to it turns the field into an output voltage proportional to that current, AC or DC. Two Hall plates cancel uniform stray fields, and an internal shield cuts coupling from fast voltage swings on the conductor. It runs from one 4.5 V to 5.5 V supply with a ratiometric output, about 120 kHz bandwidth and gain and offset trimmed over temperature at the factory. The family covers ±50 A, ±100 A and ±150 A bidirectional and 50 A, 100 A and 150 A unidirectional versions; ACS780LLRTR-100B-T is the ±100 A, 20 mV/A, -40 °C to 150 °C version. The family is marked not for new design (March 14, 2025), with ACS37220 named as its replacement.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The current to be measured enters IP+ and leaves IP-, through the package's own conductor. The chip runs from 5 V with a 0.1 µF bypass from VCC to GND. VOUT goes through RF to the output, with CF from the output to ground forming a low-pass filter that trims noise; RF and CF are sized for the application. The output sits at VCC/2 with no current and moves linearly with current in either direction, AC or DC.

operation.text: The ACS780xLR family was classed not for new design on March 14, 2025; it remains in production for existing customers, samples are no longer offered, and ACS37220 is the named substitute.

A low-offset linear Hall IC sits close to a copper conduction path inside the package. The field of the current in that path is converted to a voltage. Sensitivity and quiescent output are trimmed in production, and chopper stabilization with digital temperature compensation keeps them steady over temperature. Two Hall plates reject a field common to both.
Bidirectional versions rest at VCC/2 and unidirectional versions at 0.1 × VCC with no current (2.5 V and 0.5 V at VCC = 5 V). Rising current from IP+ (pin 5) to IP- (pin 6) drives the output upward.

The current path has 200 µΩ typical resistance and is thick enough to survive large overcurrents. Its terminals are electrically separate from signal pins 1 to 4 and 7, so the primary may sit at up to 100 V peak. An integrated shield reduces capacitive coupling from fast dV/dt on the conductor to the die, which keeps output ripple and offset drift low in high-side, high-voltage use.
Lead (Pb) free: leads plated with 100 % matte tin and no lead inside. The leadframe is heavy-gauge oxygen-free copper. Fully calibrated before shipment.

These sequences hold at 25 °C with no output load and no significant field. While VCC ramps up the output is high impedance. Once VCC passes VPORH a counter runs for tPORR; the output leaves high impedance only when that time has passed and VCC is also above VUVLOH, then settles to its normal level (VCC/2 with no current) after tUVLOD, 14 µs in this sequence. On the way down, the output goes high impedance once VCC falls below VPORL.

Below VCC(min) = 4.5 V: if VCC falls below VUVLOL a counter starts; if VCC is still below VUVLOL after tUVLOE, the output is pulled to near GND. If VCC recovers above VUVLOL before then, the output carries on at VCC/2. From lockout, VCC rising above VUVLOH releases the output after tUVLOD. If VCC drops below VPORL before tUVLOE ends, the output goes straight to high impedance.

The trim EEPROM is protected with Hamming-code error checking and correction, active after power-up. On an error that cannot be corrected, VOUT goes high impedance and the part stops responding to field.

The Hall signal is modulated so the offset and the wanted signal sit at different frequencies; demodulation returns the signal to baseband and pushes the offset up, where a filter removes it. Sample-and-hold demodulation at a high clock rate gives low thermal and stress drift, lower noise and a stable quiescent output after temperature cycling. The chopping frequency is 500 kHz.

Power-on time tPO: from VCC reaching its minimum operating value to the output settling within ±10 % of its final value under an applied field. Rise time tr: output going from 10 % to 90 % of full scale. Response time tRESPONSE: from the applied current reaching 80 % of its final value to the output reaching 80 % of its matching value. Propagation delay tPD: input current at 20 % to output at 20 % of final value. Eddy-current losses in the IC's conductive ground plane lengthen tr and tRESPONSE.

Common-mode rejection works best when external fields fall equally on both Hall plates. A nearby trace's error depends on its distance d from the IC centre, its width w and its angle θ; keep θ near 90°, or if that cannot be done keep d as large as possible. Other stray-field sources are the traces leading to the integrated conductor and nearby permanent magnets.
The traces feeding IP+ and IP- should arrive within an angle of 0° to 85°; a trace outside that range adds stray field and is treated as a nearby current path.

A current trace that runs too far under the package along the IP bus changes how current flows in the bus, alters the coupling factor and can badly degrade accuracy. Simulation shows a stronger field at Hall plate H1 when the trace stops at the intended point.
